refuted.fact: F69 and event_date_basis: 'The PDF's internal creation timestamp is D:20260320231147Z, matching the 2026-03-20 filing.'
refuted.why: False. The govinfo/CFTC PDF's /CreationDate is D:20260321130445Z and /ModDate is D:20260321090452-04'00' -- both 2026-03-21, the day AFTER filing. D:20260320231147Z is the /M value carried on the PDF's link Annot objects, not a document timestamp. It was recorded as first-party corroboration of the 2026-03-20 filing date and corroborates nothing; 2026-03-20 23:11:47Z is also about 14 hours after the 08:45 filing. Delete the sentence. The filing date stands on '[FR Doc. 2026-05635 Filed 3-20-26; 8:45 am]' alone, which I confirmed in both the .txt endpoint and the PDF.

refuted.fact: sourcing_notes and unverified_or_excluded: 'No PDF text extraction is possible in this container (pdftotext and pdftoppm are both absent)' / 'the PDF could not be converted to text'.
refuted.why: False. pypdf and pdfminer are both installed and importable. I ran PdfReader on govinfo.pdf and got all 20 pages, 161,882 characters. Consequence: source #1 of 3 is a document the researcher cited without ever reading, verified only by md5 identity. I did read it and it does corroborate the .txt endpoint -- including the stray 'li' in the masthead. The researcher abandoned an available route and then recorded the abandonment as a container limitation.

unsupported.fact: F61: 'SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins launched Project Crypto on July 31, 2025'.
unsupported.why: Announcement-date vs document-date conflation. The release never gives a launch date. It says Atkins launched Project Crypto 'In connection with the release of the report' (the PWG Report of July 30, 2025). July 31, 2025 is the date of the SPEECH cited in footnote 18 ('American Leadership in the Digital Finance Revolution (July 31, 2025)'). The rest of F61 (PWG Report 30 July 2025; the 29 January 2026 joint Atkins/Selig announcement) I confirmed verbatim.

unsupported.fact: event_date_basis and editorial_brief: the effective date equals the publication date BECAUSE it is an interpretive rule exempt from notice and comment and so could take effect immediately under 5 U.S.C. 808(2).
unsupported.why: The causal 'because' is the researcher's inference, not the source's statement. The release says only that, notwithstanding OMB's 'major rule' designation, the interpretation 'may take effect immediately pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 808(2) because it is an interpretive rule and thus exempt from the Administrative Procedure Act's notice and comment requirements'. It never explains why DATES reads 23 March. The editorial_brief instructs the writer to put this causal sentence in the article, so it must be softened to what the source says.

unsupported.fact: F03 second sentence ('The Federal Register's own agencies metadata likewise lists...') and F04 second sentence ('The Federal Register classifies the document type as Rule').
unsupported.why: Traceability failure, not falsity. Both are true -- I confirmed agencies=[CFTC, SEC] and type='Rule' -- but they come from https://www.federalregister.gov/api/v1/documents/2026-05635.json, which is NOT one of the three listed sources, while the facts are attached to the .txt endpoint. The .txt shows only the section heading '[Rules and Regulations]', not a type field. Either add the API URL to sources or drop the metadata sentences.

unsupported.fact: F06: 'The interpretation was signed on 2026-03-17 by the secretaries of both agencies.'
unsupported.why: Slight overread of the signature block. It reads 'By the Commissions. / Dated: March 17, 2026.' above the two secretaries' names -- the Commissions acted and the secretaries attest. Accurate phrasing: 'issued by the two Commissions and dated 17 March 2026, attested by the two secretaries'. The date itself is fully confirmed and also appears in both CFR table entries (F08, confirmed).

additional_findings: MATERIAL OMISSION -- footnote 7 is arguably the most consequential legal move in the release and appears nowhere in the 70 facts: 'To the extent the Commission's opinion in In re Barkate, Release No. 34-49542, 2004 WL 762434, at *3 n.13 (Apr. 8, 2004), or other such prior statements by the Commission or its staff indicate that the Commission does not view commonality as a requirement for an investment contract under Howey, the Commission concludes and clarifies that, based on courts' post-Barkate decisions, the common enterprise element must be satisfied.' The Commission is expressly reversing its own 2004 position.

MATERIAL OMISSION -- footnote 81, directly relevant to Taiwanese readers using overseas stablecoins: payment stablecoins issued by a 'foreign permitted stablecoin issuer' registered with the Comptroller of the Currency will generally NOT meet the definition of 'security', because they will generally be Covered Stablecoins (section 18 of the GENIUS Act).

MATERIAL OMISSION -- footnote 142: the airdrop interpretation 'does not apply to or otherwise affect existing Commission or staff positions regarding employee compensation and benefit arrangements involving the issuance or award of securities.'

MATERIAL OMISSION -- footnote 89: the third-party-representations carve-out has an exception. 'Where the third party and the issuer collude to convey representations or promises, it would be reasonable for a purchaser to expect profits based on those explicit representations or promises.' F31 records only the rule, not the exception.

MATERIAL OMISSION -- footnote 127 is broader than the four named Ancillary Services: 'To the extent that Service Providers provide services not discussed below, their activities are outside the scope of this release.' This strengthens the must_not_write line about not turning 'outside the scope' into 'is a security' or 'is now allowed'.

MATERIAL OMISSION -- the stablecoin conclusion is time-conditioned: 'These crypto assets categorically will not be securities by operation of statute AFTER THE EFFECTIVE DATE of the GENIUS Act.' Today the basis is the Commission's Howey interpretation of Covered Stablecoins, not the statute. F28 gets close but omits this sentence.
